I don't know if it's the same stuff, but while working at a manufacturing facility over the summer to help make some money during my college years, I had a horrible experience with yellow paint. "Safety Yellow" it was called, and our job was to paint things around the plant that needed to be safety yellow. Doors, poles, rails; whatever.

That paint... I literally don't know what it was made of. It was thick, and somehow sticky. Not sticky like you'd expect paint to be, but rather tacky. It seemed when it dried on literally any surface except the surface we were supposed to be painting, it would not actually dry, and the stuff was like glitter. No matter what you did, no matter how hard you'd try to clean it off, if you got any on your hands or a finger or a few spots on your shirt, it *would* find its way, streaked onto your phone or your wallet or pop up on your steering wheel in your vehicle and always magically end up on your skin in the shower two days later.

For four years I worked with that stuff, and I hated every second of it. Give me the red paint for the heavy fire doors, or the blue paint for the walls, or even the silver and tar paint on the roof; anything but that goddamn yellow paint. That stuff was sentient and chaotic evil.

Sorta related; I was around 5 or 6 I think and it was my younger sibling's birthday. We had lots of family over. My house at the time was a single-floor ranch style, and we had a basement. 

The birthday party festivities were happening in the basement; that's where pretty much everyone was. I had to use the bathroom, so I went up the stairs, turned right and then right again to get to the hallway, and started walking down to the bathroom.

I remember it being early to mid evening; not super dark but the sun had mostly gone down. It was May so probably around 6:00 or 7:00 pm? Anyway, in order to get to the bathroom you have to walk by my sibling's room.

As I walked by the room I casually looked in; the door was open so it just seemed natural to do so. Inside it was dark, but it was light enough outside that I could see.... something sitting on the bed. It was silhouetted against the window. I recall it being hairy looking, almost like a fictional creature (but again; it was just its silhouette so there were no details or color; it was just black). And its eyes were glowing kinda like a cat's; not supernaturally but nocturnally, if that makes sense.

I saw it and then kept walking; didn't even see it for longer than a second. I got to the bathroom, terrified by what I saw, but did my business. Then I had to get back to the party. And I did so; went right by the room. Only this time I didn't look in; just very quickly hustled back to the kitchen area and to the stairs.

No idea what I saw, why I saw it, what it could mean, or anything. I DO know that we were keeping coats on top of the bed, but I don't recall it looking like a coat; it was upright. Whatever it was until I was at least in high school whenever I'd walk by that room at night I'd look into it. Never saw it or anything like it again, so frankly I have no clue.

Eh.... as one with a biology degree, I took an animal behavior class, and a well-known gorilla was part of one of the lessons. I have to say, after reading over some of the transcripts of her "conversations" with her trainer, I found it extremely, well, not definitive. Most of the stuff was the gorilla signing some seemingly random word, and then her trainer "interpreted" that to mean something specific. And I wasn't sold on it.

Here's an example; part of a transcript from an online chat. As I understand, people were able to ask questions, and the gorilla's trainer would interpret her signs for the audience. The moderator for the chat was a user. You can read the whole thing online.

>Question: A user asks: Would the gorilla like to have a kitten, a dog, or another gorilla as a friend?

>LiveGorilla: dog

>Trainer: She actually has two dog friends right now, one kitty, and two gorillas.

>Moderator: Another user asks: What are the names of your kittens? (and dogs?)
   
>LiveGorilla: foot
   
>Trainer: Foot isn't the name of your kitty.
   
>Moderator: Gorilla, what's the name of your cat?
   
>LiveGorilla: no
   
>Trainer: She just gave some vocalizations there... some soft puffing.
   
>Moderator: I heard that soft puffing!
   
>Trainer: Now shaking her head no.
   
>Question: Do you like to chat with other people?
   
>Moderator: That was from another user!
   
>LiveGorilla: fine nipple
   
>Trainer: Nipple rhymes with people; she doesn't sign people per se, she was trying to do a "sounds like..."

Now, the gorilla answers one question perfectly reasonably; when asked if she'd like a kitten, dog, or gorilla friend, she says dog. Okay. But then she very incorrectly answers a question, then apparently refuses to answer, and then the trainer gives an interpretation of her "fine nipple" response that swings it to something like "these are fine people" or "it's fine to talk to these people" or whatever.

Here's another example.

>Moderator: How do you feel about a certain male?
   
>LiveGorilla: foot, foot, good
   
>Moderator: foot means male, right?
   
>LiveGorilla: nipple
   
>Trainer: Remember that foot=male, right.
   
>LiveGorilla: good
   
>Trainer: She's acting out a little here.
   
>Moderator: What about another male?
   
>LiveGorilla: bad
   
>Moderator: Oh dear.
   
>LiveGorilla: toilet
   
>Moderator: Uh oh!
   
>Trainer: That's her word for bad!
   
>Moderator: I thought he was supposed to be her mate! What did he do to you today, gorilla?
   
>Trainer: I don't know... she doesn't have good things to say about him today.
   
>LiveGorilla: down
   
>Trainer: What did he do today? He did something obnoxious that was obnoxious, but I didn't see what happened. Maybe they had a little tiff.

Again; there's implications here I suppose, but it's so not definitive to me. I don't want to be *that person* trying to claim that the gorilla is all a hoax and none of this is real; I think there is *something* there, but certainly when people act like she was a fluent signer and could really speak to us, I don't think that's really true at all.

It can be used in spellcasting as well as the creation of magical items and writing magical spells. Real currency can be broken down and used in spellwork and for copying spells like any other component, the coins breaking down easily into impure magical dust when exposed to the twists of arcana accompanying a spell. On an earth-sized planet, you can technically see out to about 3 miles max before the ground curves away beyond the horizon, but that doesn't account for things like trees or mountains blocking your view (3 miles at sea, basically). But we obviously can't make out fine details at 3 miles.

The Eagle Aspect of the Beast that certain character classes can get at level 6 lets them see **fine details** (as if they were standing 100 feet away) out to even a mile. This implies that most characters cannot see fine details that far away. The game master’s screen has rules on visibility as well; on a clear day with no obstructions, the average person can see 2 miles out. When raining, this goes down to 1 mile. Fog reduces visibility to 100-300 feet, and when you are on a structure or up in the air, these distances are multiplied by 20 (which I think is a bit much; you'd have to do your best with this. Even on a tower, I don't think a player character could see 40 miles out; that's far beyond the limits of the horizon even from a height). Regardless, these numbers imply that a player character could spot a caravan or a group of herd animals from those distances but no farther. They wouldn't be able to make out the insignia on the banners trailing from their wagons or what kind of animals they are.

By the rules as written, a human at night wouldn't be able to see more than a few feet in front of them without some form of light; darkness (and even a moonlit night qualifies as darkness) creates a heavily obscured area, and creatures in a heavily obscured area are effectively blinded. At twilight and dawn, you have dim light, at which point by the rules as written, I think the human can see up to the distances I described above (2 miles in clear weather, 1 mile in rain, etc.) but have disadvantage on their perception checks.

There is no such thing as "dim vision" in the current edition, though you can house rule what you like. There is only darkvision. Darkvision works like this; you have a range associated with your darkvision, most commonly 60 feet as you mention. Think about it as a bubble that is 60 feet in radius with you at the center; any dim light within that bubble is considered bright light for a creature with darkvision; they can see perfectly fine. Any darkness within that bubble is considered dim light; they have disadvantage on attack rolls. Beyond that 60-foot range, darkvision does not work at all. So if you had a character with darkvision standing in a pitch-black dungeon, they can see things within 60 feet as if they were in dim light, rather than darkness. Anything at 61 feet or farther away is in pitch-black darkness; the character cannot see them. A human, meanwhile, would be effectively blind in such a situation.

- Changed **Scoped** modification to **Long Barrel** modification. Added heavy property to *Long Barrel*.

- Changed **Targeting** modification to **Sighted** modification.

- Added the **Handheld** modification, allowing an artificer to wield their Thunder Cannon in one hand at the cost of reduced power. Allows for niche character concepts such as wielding a gun and sword together while retaining a level of balance.
